tickets.text: Option B from ^report(5): evaluate each livelit's view in the worker, keep the last Html sent per livelit, and post patches to it, so view evaluation leaves the main thread. Needs the view runner (ViewCmdRunner) in the worker, a patch format, an element on the page that owns each livelit's DOM and applies patches, and handlers dispatched by id. Keep the page's own path for an interaction's immediate redraw, or every drag waits a round trip. Its condition is now met (2026-10-12, see ^ticket(10)): evaluating the view is about 69% of the main thread in a woods figure move, and C would save about 2%. Weigh it against making the view itself cheaper first (^ticket(1), ^ticket(2)). PROTOTYPED 2026-10-14 (local branches, nothing pushed; work notes http://matthewhammer.org/hazel-work-notes/work-notes/2026/10/14/2026-10-14T2120-0600.html): MvuShape and ViewCmdRunner moved to the language library (61d031fd93, no change in behavior); the worker runs view commands to Html, reusing an unchanged view per projector (fast_equal), and whole programs fold their views in too (experiments on experiment/2635-views-in-worker-all, ede920b07e). Full Body: the main thread about 540 ms (UX mode) / 220 ms (whole program) less per change, the redraw no later; Kids' Choice: release about 45 ms later (144 → 187–196 ms). Waits for Matthew's design calls: which livelits' views move (all, or the costly ones), and the on-screen ids in the request. 2026-10-15T18:52: tagged 🪷 blocked on Matthew: its next step is his call (see above).

tickets.area: dress up -> hazel, the port: a plan, and a report on drawing, music and menus
tickets.text:
Plan the port of Messed Up Dress Up to Hazel, and a report today on its three hardest questions. Matthew: "a ticket that plans a port of Messed Up Dress Up to Hazel" and "I'm especially interested in a report today answering the following questions:"
  • "what parts of Messed Up Dress Up drawing would be most challenging for Hazel?"
  • "can we do music in Hazel?"
  • "how would we offer the complex menu system while still doing 'Always be Knowlling'? -- even tho we can hide the program and show only livelits, they do not follow our protocol in Messed Up Dress UP for menu design."
Builds on: ^du_report(8), Piece by piece (^ticket(359), published this morning: the port, feature by feature, in two months or three); ^report(15) (Dress Up and its livelits side by side, measured); ^du_report(5)'s menu guidance, Always Be Knolling (^ticket(375)). The report likely goes in the Dress Up series as the next ^du_report, with what it measures or tries in Hazel (a drawing, a sound) shown, not only argued. Not blocked on Matthew: the earlier ask, ^ticket(359), is done. 11:14, Matthew, a subsection: "Let's have a subsection that summarizes 'advanced' features of MUDU (world design, animated click to walk, click to sit, etc.) --- and stages them as challenges for Hazel." So the report also lists the game's advanced features (the world designer, click to walk with its animation, click to sit, and the rest) and puts them in stages, easiest first, each as a challenge for Hazel: what it would take there, and what stands in the way. Expanded, 2026-10-20: Matthew: "But let's expand the story: Drawing pictures with Hazel code (to create Html.T instances) is not fast enough for doing MUDU via Hazel, yet. But MUDU could be scripted with Hazel, for game logic --- let's examine this claim with data. Things like: * when we pull a lever (an event in the MVC system), we do a monadic command to change the trapdoor it links with, under some table we project from. * the table has all lever-thing connections. Trapdoors for now." So: test the claim with data. Hazel is not yet fast enough to draw Dress Up's pictures (Html.T), but may be fast enough for its game logic, for example: a lever pulled (an event in the MVU loop) runs a monadic command that changes the trapdoor the lever is linked to, found in a table of lever-to-thing connections (trapdoors for now), a projected table. Measure what such a rule costs to evaluate, against the game's frame budget. Related: ^ticket(473), the agenda's item 11. Matthew: "^ Related. https://arxiv.org/html/1703.05410v1": the lever rule in the paper's terms is a player intent (pull) whose mechanics rule, a step from state and intent to state and response, reads the connections table; the comparison is ^report(20)'s item 11. Matthew, next: "the main wrinkle for Hazel matching the script shape we want --- we need global variables for simple games --- most scripts use them. So we need to be monadic." So the rules read and write the game's globals through commands (a state monad), and the measurement includes that.

tickets.text: Ideation: Hazel as the editor of a Scratch-like game-building environment, with Messed Up Dress Up as its world, people and objects; partly blocked on Matthew. Matthew: "Ideation, partly blocked on Matthew, about Hazel as the editor for a Scratch-like game-building environment, based on Messed Up Dress Up as the world/people/object system. Livelits show that hazel can express a lot, but not yet with adequate performance to play the role of the "game engine" and the "drawing logic". But the "game logic", especially simple event-based declarations: When this action in game happens, this other action is queued to happen (perhaps immediately). If we can expose Hazel tiles within Messed Up Dress Up to customize behavior, we'll have a synergistic configuration to drive more play and research, and their combination." So: Dress Up keeps its engine and its drawing (JavaScript, at 60 fps); Hazel tiles, inside Dress Up, declare the game logic, as events and the actions they queue ("when this happens, then that"), small enough for Hazel's evaluator today. tickets.text: The moon and the sun as they really are: pick a place on Earth (a GPS coordinate) and see the sky there on the game's date, mapped to real-world dates. Matthew: "mint and enqueue for MUDU, low priority for the day, but important this weekend: * moon cycles. Seeing the moon accurately, during the cycle. Selecting a GPS coordinate and seeing the moon in the sky accurately at that GPS coordinate during the game's idea of its date (mapped to real world dates). * sun cycles (winter, spring, summer, winter). Same idea." Today the game has no date and no place: a few places have their own time-of-day choice (fallTime, campTime, fairyTime: day, sunrise, sunset, night), and the moon is drawn the same way every time. To do: the game's date and time (mapped to real dates); a place, picked with the chip box (a few named places, or a latitude and longitude); the moon's phase, its height and its direction, and the sun's height and direction, worked out on the device (no network, so it works in airplane mode); the moon drawn lit as its phase is, where it stands in the scene's sky; the seasons from the sun (day length, the sun's height at noon); each place's time-of-day choice following the clock, or kept as it is. So: the place is chosen in the game, never read from the device (no location, no device clock); the backgrounds with times of day (the campsite, the fall woods, the fairy forest, ...) take their day length and their sun's and moon's places from that place and the game's date, roughly right rather than exact.

tickets.progress: ^report(25) 'What a Call into Hazel Costs' drafted locally (hazel-perf-report c8783e0, work in progress, not published). Cause: (1) the World rule's find is annotated ([Cell], Int, Int), and Hazel re-checks that type over the rest of the list on every recursive call: quadratic, 153 ms at 16x16 (22.6 without the annotation); (2) every call converts the argument to unevaluated syntax with fresh UUIDs and re-evaluates it, ~31 us per cell; (3) ~3 us per evaluator step. Passing only the neighbouring cells: ~0.9 ms at every size. tickets.area: hazel, performance: why #2681 raises a library call's floor by about a quarter (^report(25))
tickets.source: Matthew, 2026-10-22 07:30, in chat, after ^report(25)'s before-and-after update
tickets.text: Find why #2681 makes every library call's floor about 25% slower, and whether it can skip recording values it will never see again. Matthew: "Yes: find why #2681 raises the floor by about a quarter, and whether it can skip recording values it will never see again." ^report(25) measured, in two rounds: a Hazel rule that ignores its argument costs 8.5 ms at 16x16 before #2681 and 10.1-10.6 ms with it (19.3 to 25.3 ms at 24x24), while the annotated rule gets 7-16x faster. The argument is converted afresh by of_js on every call, so #2681's memo records values it can never reuse.
tickets.progress: 07:30: minted and started. | 07:37: COUNTED (WeakMap get/set wrapped in node around GitHub's #2681 build, no rebuild): per 16x16 identity call, #2681 does 4,137 memo lookups (all miss), 2,580 memo writes (1,280 list tails: the cells' and every cell's ways; 1,041 record fields; 258 records) and 6,734 type-hash lookups; the shipped rule's whole win is 137 hits, one per step of find. Switching off only the writes does NOT lower the floor; without them the shipped rule is ~30% slower than before #2681, so the per-check lookups are the cost (plus GC: 2.7 ms of a 10 ms floor before #2681). FIX TRIED: trial/r25-2681-depth (5b79ba5f95): has_type asked and told only at depth 0 and 1 of a pushed value (find's list is a part of its tuple, depth 1). GitHub's Deploy building; then floor.sh times before / #2681 / depth, three rounds with GC time. | 07:47: FOUND AND FIXED ON A TRIAL BRANCH. Why: #2681 asks its memo (and #2661's type-hash cache) at every part of every pushed value, and records every part and every tail; a library call's argument is new each call, so none of it is asked again. Skipping only the writes does not help (identity 9.6-9.9 vs 9.7 ms); GC is not it (2.45 / 2.54 / 2.39 ms per call). Fix: trial/r25-2681-depth (5b79ba5f95), memo asked and told only at depth 0 and 1 (Ascriptions.memo_depth = 1). Per 16x16 identity call: 6 lookups / 3 writes / 8 type-hash lookups (was 4,137 / 2,580 / 6,734); shipped keeps 136 of 137 hits.
